## Statement

Consider a hypothetical homogeneous three-dimensional gas with particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin, number density $n_0>0$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, translational temperature $T_0>0$ in kelvins, and a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as the velocity density below. Put $\theta=k_BT_0/m$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $V_c=\sqrt{3\theta}$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and define the prepared number density in velocity space by

$$f_0(v)=\frac{n_0}{8V_c^3}\,\mathbf 1_{[-V_c,V_c]^3}(v),\qquad v\in\mathbb R^3.$$

The density $f_0$ has units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$, so $f_0\,d^3v$ is a number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

Here $\mathbf 1_C$ is the function equal to one on the cube $C$ and zero outside it. The corresponding Maxwellian with the same number density, zero mean velocity, and temperature $T_0$ is

$$M(v)=n_0\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT_0}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{m|v|^2}{2k_BT_0}\right).$$

Define the dimensionless weighted norm by $\|g\|_{1,3}=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|v/v_*|^3)|g(v)|\,d^3v$, where $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Under the homogeneous fast-scale conserving BGK model with $\tau>0$ seconds and dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$, this preparation has an exact initial-layer solution: for every fixed $t>0$, $f^\varepsilon(t)\to M$ in this weighted $L^1$ norm as $\varepsilon\to0$, while $f^\varepsilon(0)=f_0\ne M$. The compactly supported $f_0$ is a hypothetical distribution, not an observed preparation or experiment.

## Statement references

[François Golse and C. David Levermore, Fluid Dynamics from Kinetic Equations, Lecture 2, “The BGK Operator”](https://www.cmls.polytechnique.fr/perso/golse/Exposes/HLslides2.pdf)

[David Tong, Lectures on Kinetic Theory, §2.5.1 (relaxation-time approximation and its non-exactness qualification)](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/kintheory/two.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n_0,T_0,m,k_B,\tau,\varepsilon,f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the units and dimensionless conventions in the statement, the hypothetical $f_0$, and the homogeneous BGK model.

[F1] [[pthm-fd-bgk-equilibration]] (current same-batch draft physics theorem; its K01 mathematical suppliers, including [[thm-fd-homogeneous-bgk-limit]] and [[prop-fd-bgk-entropy-rate]], are current draft carriers with Step 1 readiness records marked ready, recording authoring readiness but not proof acceptance): for nonnegative initial data with finite $\omega_3$ moment, positive number density and centered second moment, and finite reference-relative entropy, the homogeneous fast-scale BGK solution has the exact formula and weighted-norm equality in its Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Let $C=n_0/(8V_c^3)$ and $R=\sqrt3V_c/v_*$. The cube has volume $8V_c^3$, so $\int f_0\,d^3v=n_0$. Symmetry of each interval gives $\int v f_0\,d^3v=0$. For the second moment, each coordinate contributes $(2V_c)^2\int_{-V_c}^{V_c}s^2\,ds=8V_c^5/3$, so $\int_{[-V_c,V_c]^3}|v|^2\,d^3v=8V_c^5$; dividing by $8V_c^3$ gives mean square speed $V_c^2$. Thus $\int |v|^2f_0\,d^3v=n_0V_c^2=3n_0k_BT_0/m$, so the mean velocity is zero and its temperature is $T_0$. On the support, $\omega_3(v)\le1+R+R^2+R^3$, hence $\int\omega_3 f_0\,d^3v\le n_0(1+R+R^2+R^3)<\infty$. With $f_{\rm ref}>0$ in the same units as $C$, $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,d^3v=n_0|\log(C/f_{\rm ref})|<\infty$, using $0\log0=0$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The Maxwellian $M$ is strictly positive on all of $\mathbb R^3$, whereas $f_0$ vanishes outside the compact cube, so $f_0\ne M$ almost everywhere and $\|f_0-M\|_{1,3}>0$. The data in step 1.1 satisfy the hypotheses of [F1]; applying it gives the exact solution and exponential weighted-norm equality. [given, F1, step 1.1]

3.1 For each fixed $t>0$, $e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, so the equality in step 2.1 gives $f^\varepsilon(t)\to M$ in weighted $L^1$. At $t=0$, the solution is $f_0$, whose positive mismatch was proved in step 2.1. The initial layer is therefore a conditional model prediction for this hypothetical preparation, not an empirical result. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and
$\omega_3(v)=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$. Let
$f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable velocity number density,
with $f_0$ in $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$ and $f_0\,d^3v$ measured in
$\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, satisfying
$\int\omega_3 f_0\,d^3v<\infty$, number density
$n_0=\int f_0\,d^3v>0$, positive centered second moment, and finite
reference-relative entropy $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,d^3v$, where
$f_{\rm ref}>0$ is constant in the same units as $f_0$. Take the primitive
particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per
kelvin. Define $u_0=n_0^{-1}\int v f_0\,d^3v$ and
$T_0=m(3k_Bn_0)^{-1}\int |v-u_0|^2f_0\,d^3v>0$. For any nonnegative velocity
density $g$ with finite $\omega_3$ moment, number density
$n[g]=\int g\,d^3v>0$, and positive centered second moment, define
$u[g]=n[g]^{-1}\int vg\,d^3v$,
$T[g]=m(3k_Bn[g])^{-1}\int|v-u[g]|^2g\,d^3v$, and its normalized
moment-matched Maxwellian

$$M[g](v)=n[g]\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT[g]}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{m|v-u[g]|^2}{2k_BT[g]}\right).$$

Write $M=M[f_0]$; it has the same number, momentum, and kinetic-energy
moments as $f_0$.
For $\tau>0$ in seconds and dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$, consider the
homogeneous equation

$$\partial_t f^\varepsilon(v,t)=\frac{M[f^\varepsilon](v,t)-f^\varepsilon(v,t)}{\varepsilon\tau},\qquad f^\varepsilon(v,0)=f_0(v),\quad t\ge0.$$

There is a nonnegative solution
$f^\varepsilon\in C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v))$ given by

$$f^\varepsilon(v,t)=M(v)+e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)).$$

It solves the equation in $L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v)$ and preserves the number,
momentum, and kinetic-energy moments of $f_0$. It is also the unique solution
in the following pointwise class: a jointly measurable
$\tilde f:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with finite
$\omega_3$-weighted velocity integral at every time and initial trace
$\tilde f(v,0)=f_0(v)$ for almost every $v$, whose velocity sections are
continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ for almost
every $v$. Require a common full-measure set of velocities on which the
equation holds for every $t>0$, and, on each compact time interval, an
integrable $\omega_3$-weighted majorant for $\partial_t\tilde f$ independent
of $t$. Also require the density and temperature of $\tilde f$ to remain
positive. These envelopes permit differentiation of the three moment
integrals and justify the conservation argument in the proof.

For each $T_*>0$, with the dimensionless fixed velocity weight
$\|g\|_{1,3}=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|v/v_*|^3)|g(v)|\,d^3v$, it satisfies

$$\|f^\varepsilon(t)-M\|_{1,3}=e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\|f_0-M\|_{1,3},\qquad \int_0^{T_*}\|f^\varepsilon(t)-M\|_{1,3}\,dt\le\varepsilon\tau\|f_0-M\|_{1,3}.$$

Writing $H(g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g\log(g/f_{\rm ref})\,d^3v$ with $0\log0:=0$, the entropy
gap obeys

$$0\le H(f^\varepsilon(t))-H(M)\le e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\bigl(H(f_0)-H(M)\bigr).$$

Thus for each fixed $t>0$, $f^\varepsilon(t)\to M$ in this weighted $L^1$
norm as $\varepsilon\to0$, while $f^\varepsilon(0)=f_0$; if $f_0$ differs
from $M$ on a set of positive measure, the initial mismatch is nonzero. If
$f_0=M$ almost everywhere, the formula gives the stationary equilibrium with
zero norm and entropy gaps. This is an exact homogeneous BGK model prediction
and does not assert an inhomogeneous Boltzmann-to-Euler limit or an observed
relaxation.

## Statement references

[François Golse and C. David Levermore, Fluid Dynamics from Kinetic Equations, Lecture 2, “The BGK Operator”](https://www.cmls.polytechnique.fr/perso/golse/Exposes/HLslides2.pdf)

[David Tong, Lectures on Kinetic Theory, §2.5.1 (relaxation-time approximation and its non-exactness qualification)](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/kintheory/two.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nonnegative initial density, its finite $\omega_3$ moment and entropy, positive number density and centered second moment, $\varepsilon,\tau>0$, and the homogeneous fast-scale BGK equation.

[F1] [[thm-fd-homogeneous-bgk-limit]] (current batch-25 draft carrier; its Step 1 readiness record is present and marked ready, recording authoring readiness but not proof acceptance): for the stated $\omega_3$-integrable initial data and positive moments, the solution is in $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v))$, has the exact formula $M+e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}(f_0-M)$, and satisfies the $\omega_3$-weighted equality and integrated bound in its Statement.

[F2] [[def-fd-conserving-bgk]]: the BGK operator is $(M[f]-f)/\tau$, with $M[f]$ the Maxwellian of the exact number, mean-velocity, and positive-temperature moments.

[F3] [[prop-fd-maxwellian-moments]]: the Maxwellian has exactly the number, momentum, and kinetic-energy moments used to define it.

[F4] [[prop-fd-bgk-entropy-rate]] (current batch-25 draft carrier; its Step 1 readiness record is present and marked ready, recording authoring readiness but not proof acceptance): under the hypotheses of the exact homogeneous relaxation theorem, $0\le H(f^\varepsilon(t))-H(M)\le e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}(H(f_0)-H(M))$.

[F5] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: a common integrable derivative majorant permits differentiating each invariant moment integral.

[F6] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and [[thm-chain-rule]]: the exponential is differentiable with derivative itself, and differentiating its composition with a scalar multiple applies the chain rule.

[F7] [[def-derivative]] and [[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]]: the derivative is a difference-quotient limit, and products of existing limits have the product limit.

[F8] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there, by applying the theorem to any compact subinterval.

[A1] The initial-data, pointwise-solution, positivity, derivative-envelope, and model assumptions in the Statement hold.

[A2] [[post-fd-bgk-relaxation]]: for $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v))$ trajectories, the adopted equation holds in that weighted Banach space at every $t\ge0$; for the pointwise solution class stated here, it holds for every $t>0$ on one common full-measure set of velocities. In both senses it is the separate moment-preserving BGK model with relaxation time $\tau>0$, not the binary Boltzmann collision operator.

## Proof

1.1 The initial data and parameters meet the hypotheses of [F1]. It supplies the explicit solution in the weighted Banach space and its $\omega_3$ estimate. The BGK definition [F2] and Gaussian moment result [F3] use the same positive number density, momentum, and kinetic energy as the Statement. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Let $\tilde f$ be any solution in the pointwise class stated above. By [F5], its number, momentum, and energy moment functions are differentiable under their integrals. Integrating the equation [A2] against $1$, $mv_i$, and $m|v|^2/2$, the BGK definition [F2] and Maxwellian moments [F3] make each derivative zero. Hence those moments equal their initial values, so $M[\tilde f(t)]=M$ for every $t$. The equation reduces to $\partial_t(\tilde f-M)=-(\tilde f-M)/(\varepsilon\tau)$ for almost every velocity and every $t>0$. [given, A1, A2, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 For almost every $v$, set $G_v(t)=e^{t/(\varepsilon\tau)}(\tilde f(v,t)-M(v))$. By [F6]–[F7] and step 1.2, $G_v'(t)=0$ on $(0,\infty)$. Continuity at zero and [F8] imply $G_v(t)=f_0(v)-M(v)$ for all $t\ge0$. Thus every pointwise solution has the formula in step 1.1, proving uniqueness in the stated class. [given, A1, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The formula gives $|f^\varepsilon(t)-M|=e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}|f_0-M|$. Since $1+(|v|/v_*)^3\le\omega_3(v)$, the stated norm is finite and obeys the exact equality. Integrating the exponential in time gives the displayed $\varepsilon\tau$ bound. Applying [F4] to the same solution gives the entropy-gap estimate. [given, A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $t>0$, $e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\to0$; at $t=0$ the solution is $f_0$. If $f_0$ differs from $M$ on a set of positive measure, the strictly positive weight makes $\|f_0-M\|_{1,3}>0$. When $f_0=M$ almost everywhere, the formula is stationary. These are conditional predictions of the adopted BGK model [A2]. [given, A1, A2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega_3(v):=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$, let $\tau>0$ be a relaxation time in seconds, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. Let $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable velocity density with units fixed by the kinetic-density definition, with $\int\omega_3f_0\,dv<\infty$, number density $n>0$, and strictly positive centered second moment. Let $M=M[f_0]$ be its positive-temperature Gaussian from the single-species BGK definition. Fix a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f_0$ and assume $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,dv<\infty$, with $0\log0:=0$ and the integrand $f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|$ assigned value zero where $f_0=0$. Define
$$f^\epsilon(t,v):=M(v)+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)),\qquad t\ge0\text{ in seconds}.$$
Then $f^\epsilon\ge0$, has the same mass, momentum, and kinetic energy as $f_0$ for every $t$, belongs to $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$, and solves, as an equality in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$,
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=\frac{M[f^\epsilon]-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau},\qquad f^\epsilon(0)=f_0.$$
A solution means a nonnegative $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$ function satisfying this equality at each time. The solution is unique among nonnegative solutions in this function class whose density and temperature remain strictly positive. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv =e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv,$$
and for every $T_*>0$,
$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon-M|\,dv\,dt \le\epsilon\tau\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$
Thus the equilibrium limit is exact for each fixed $t>0$ and in spacetime weighted $L^1$, but need not be uniform at $t=0$. This branch has stationary homogeneous Euler moments; it gives no evolving inhomogeneous Euler limit.

## Statement references

[Tong, §2.5.1, full lecture notes](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/kintheory/two.pdf)

[Golse, §§3.1–3.2, full chapter](https://www.cmls.polytechnique.fr/perso/golse/Surveys/FGHdBookEvEq.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Nonnegative $f_0$ with finite weighted third moment and positive variance, its moment-matched Maxwellian $M$, and $\epsilon,\tau>0$.

[F1] [[def-fd-conserving-bgk]]: $Q_{\rm BGK}(f)=(M[f]-f)/\tau$.

[F2] [[prop-fd-maxwellian-moments]]: $M[f_0]$ has exactly the mass, momentum, and energy moments used to define it, and belongs to $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$.


[A1] The initial data and parameters satisfy the hypotheses in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Put $a(t)=e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}$. Then $0<a(t)\le1$ and $f^\epsilon=(1-a(t))M+ a(t)f_0$, so $f^\epsilon\ge0$. Since $M,f_0\in L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$, this formula is continuously differentiable in that Banach space and
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=-\frac{a(t)}{\epsilon\tau}(f_0-M)=\frac{M-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau}.$$
[F1, A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $\tilde f$ be any other solution in the stated class. For each invariant polynomial $\psi$ of degree at most two, the functional $\Lambda_\psi(g)=\int\psi g\,dv$ is bounded on $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$ because $|\psi(v)|\le C_\psi\omega_3(v)$. Continuity of this linear functional and the defining Banach-space derivative give $(\Lambda_\psi\circ\tilde f)\prime(t)=\Lambda_\psi(\partial_t\tilde f)$. Integrating the equation against these invariants shows each derivative is zero, because $M[\tilde f]$ and $\tilde f$ have the same defining moments by [F2]. Its moments are therefore those of $f_0$, so $M[\tilde f(t)]=M$. The equation reduces to $\partial_t(\tilde f-M)=-(\tilde f-M)/(\epsilon\tau)$ in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$. Multiplication by $e^{t/(\epsilon\tau)}$ has zero derivative, hence $\tilde f(t)=M+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0-M)=f^\epsilon(t)$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the invariant moments of $M$ and $f_0$ agree. The affine formula for $f^\epsilon$ therefore preserves them. In particular its positive number density and positive centered second moment stay fixed, so $M[f^\epsilon(t)]=M$ for every $t$. Step 1.1 is consequently the stated nonlinear BGK equation with the correct moment-matched target. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Homogeneity of the weight and the exact formula give
$$\int\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv=a(t)\int\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$
Integrating in $t$ yields the stated bound because $\int_0^{T_*}a(t)\,dt=\epsilon\tau(1-e^{-T_*/(\epsilon\tau)})\le\epsilon\tau$. For fixed $t>0$, $a(t)\to0$ as $\epsilon\to0$, whereas at $t=0$ the distance is $\int\omega_3|f_0-M|$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega_3(v)=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$, let $\tau>0$ be a relaxation time in seconds, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. Let $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable velocity density with $\int\omega_3 f_0\,dv<\infty$, number density $n=\int f_0\,dv>0$, and strictly positive centered second moment $\int|v-u_0|^2f_0\,dv>0$, where $u_0=n^{-1}\int v f_0\,dv$. Fix a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f_0$, and assume $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,dv<\infty$, using $0\log0:=0$ and assigning $f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|$ the value zero where $f_0=0$. $$f^\epsilon(t)=M+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0-M),\qquad t\ge0.$$
For each nonnegative velocity density $g$ with the same units as $f_0$ and for which the integral is absolutely finite, define
$$H(g):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(v)\log(g(v)/f_{\rm ref})\,dv,\qquad 0\log0:=0.$$
Then for every time $t\ge0$ measured in seconds,
$$0\le H(f^\epsilon(t))-H(M) \le e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}\bigl(H(f_0)-H(M)\bigr).$$
The lower bound is relative entropy with respect to the moment-matched Maxwellian. This is a deduction for the adopted BGK model and its explicit solution, not an empirical entropy measurement or a claim about the binary collision operator.

**Given:** The exact solution $f^\epsilon=M+a(t)(f_0-M)$ with $a(t)=e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}$, and equality of its mass, momentum, and energy moments with those of $M$.

[F2] [[def-fd-kinetic-density]] and [[prop-fd-maxwellian-moments]]: $\log(M/f_{\rm ref})$ is a constant plus a linear term and a quadratic term in velocity, and all its products with $f_0$ or $M$ are integrable.

[F3] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: The logarithm derivative and product rule give $\Phi\prime(z)=\log z$; its sign shows the minimum at $1$, hence $\Phi(z)\ge0$.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: On $(0,\infty)$, $\Phi''(z)=1/z>0$, so $\Phi$ is convex.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: Setting $z=e^{-y}$ gives $z\log z=-ye^{-y}\to0$ as $y\to\infty$; hence $\Phi(0)=1$ gives the continuous convex extension on $[0,\infty)$.

[A1] The nonnegative initial data has finite absolute third moment and finite absolute reference-relative entropy as in the homogeneous BGK theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Put $z_0=f_0/M$ and $\Phi(z)=z\log z-z+1$, with $\Phi(0)=1$. Since $M$ is a positive Gaussian, $\log(M/f_{\rm ref})$ is a quadratic polynomial plus a constant. The assumed finite absolute entropy and second moments make $\int f_0\log(f_0/M)$ finite; the negative part is bounded by $M/e$. Equal mass, momentum, and energy moments then give
$$H(f_0)-H(M)=\int M\Phi(z_0)\,dv<\infty.$$
At zeros of $f_0$, the formula uses $0\log0=0$; continuity of $z\log z$ at zero follows from [F5]. [A1, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 Let $a=e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}$. By [F1], $f^\epsilon/M=az_0+(1-a)$. Convexity [F4] and $\Phi(1)=0$ imply pointwise
$$0\le\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\le a\Phi(z_0).$$
Integrating against $M$ and using step 1.1 shows the relative-entropy integral is finite and
$$\int M\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\,dv\le a\bigl(H(f_0)-H(M)\bigr).$$
[F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The same moment cancellation as in step 1.1 gives
$$H(f^\epsilon)-H(M)=\int\bigl[f^\epsilon\log(f^\epsilon/M)-f^\epsilon+M\bigr]\,dv=\int M\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\,dv.$$
The identity also proves $H(f^\epsilon)$ is finite: the relative-entropy integrand is integrable by step 2.1, $\log(M/f_{\rm ref})$ grows at most quadratically, and $f^\epsilon$ has finite second moment. Nonnegativity follows from [F3]. Combining this equality with step 2.1 yields both asserted bounds. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
